chapters.title: A Guide to the Mazes of Menace
paragraphs: A Guide to the Mazes of Menace (Guidebook for NetHack)
Original version - Eric S. Raymond (Edited and expanded for NetHack 5.0.0 by Mike Stephenson and others)

chapters.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Recently, you have begun to find yourself unfulfilled and distant in your daily occupation. Strange dreams of prospecting, stealing, crusading, and combat have haunted you in your sleep for many months, but you aren't sure of the reason. You wonder whether you have in fact been having those dreams all your life, and somehow managed to forget about them until now. Some nights you awaken suddenly and cry out, terrified at the vivid recollection of the strange and powerful creatures that seem to be lurking behind every corner of the dungeon in your dream. Could these details haunting your dreams be real? As each night passes, you feel the desire to enter the mysterious caverns near the ruins grow stronger. Each morning, however, you quickly put the idea out of your head as you recall the tales of those who entered the caverns before you and did not return. Eventually you can resist the yearning to seek out the fantastic place in your dreams no longer. After all, when other adventurers came back this way after spending time in the caverns, they usually seemed better off than when they passed through the first time. And who was to say that all of those who did not return had not just kept going?

Asking around, you hear about a bauble, called the Amulet of Yendor by some, which, if you can find it, will bring you great wealth. One legend you were told even mentioned that the one who finds the amulet will be granted immortality by the gods. The amulet is rumored to be somewhere beyond the Valley of Gehennom, deep within the Mazes of Menace. Upon hearing the legends, you immediately realize that there is some profound and undiscovered reason that you are to descend into the caverns and seek out that amulet of which they spoke. Even if the rumors of the amulet's powers are untrue, you decide that you should at least be able to sell the tales of your adventures to the local minstrels for a tidy sum, especially if you encounter any of the terrifying and magical creatures of your dreams along the way. You spend one last night fortifying yourself at the local inn, becoming more and more depressed as you watch the odds of your success being posted on the inn's walls getting lower and lower.

In the morning you awake, collect your belongings, and set off for the dungeon. After several days of uneventful travel, you see the ancient ruins that mark the entrance to the Mazes of Menace. It is late at night, so you make camp at the entrance and spend the night sleeping under the open skies. In the morning, you gather your gear, eat what may be your last meal outside, and enter the dungeon....

chapters.title: What is going on here?
paragraphs: You have just begun a game of NetHack. Your goal is to grab as much treasure as you can, retrieve the Amulet of Yendor, and escape the Mazes of Menace alive.
Your abilities and strengths for dealing with the hazards of adventure will vary with your background and training:

[i]Archeologists[/i] understand dungeons pretty well; this enables them to move quickly and sneak up on the local nasties. They start equipped with the tools for a proper scientific expedition, and are able to read ancient languages.
[i]Barbarians[/i] are warriors out of the hinterland, hardened to battle. They begin their quests with naught but uncommon strength, a trusty hauberk, and a great two-handed sword.
[i]Cavemen[/i] and [i]Cavewomen[/i] start with exceptional strength but, unfortunately, with neolithic weapons.

[i]Healers[/i] are wise in medicine and apothecary. They know the herbs and simples that can restore vitality, ease pain, anesthetize, and neutralize poisons; and with their instruments, they can divine a being's state of health or sickness. Their medical practice earns them quite reasonable amounts of money, with which they enter the dungeon.
[i]Knights[/i] are distinguished from the common skirmisher by their devotion to the ideals of chivalry and by the surpassing excellence of their armor.

[i]Monks[/i] are ascetics, who by rigorous practice of physical and mental disciplines have become capable of fighting as effectively without weapons as with. They wear no armor but make up for it with increased mobility.

[i]Priests[/i] and [i]Priestesses[/i] are clerics militant, crusaders advancing the cause of righteousness with arms, armor, and arts thaumaturgic. Their ability to commune with deities via prayer occasionally extricates them from peril, but can also put them in it.
[i]Rangers[/i] are most at home in the woods, and some say slightly out of place in a dungeon. They are, however, experts in archery as well as tracking and stealthy movement.
[i]Rogues[/i] are agile and stealthy thieves, with knowledge of locks, traps, and poisons. Their advantage lies in surprise, which they employ to great advantage.
[i]Samurai[/i] are the elite warriors of feudal Nippon. They are lightly armored and quick, and wear the [i]dai-sho[/i], two swords of the deadliest keenness.
[i]Tourists[/i] start out with lots of gold (suitable for shopping with), a credit card, lots of food, some maps, and an expensive camera. Most monsters don't like being photographed.
[i]Valkyries[/i] are hardy warrior women. Their upbringing in the harsh Northlands makes them strong, inures them to extremes of cold, and instills in them stealth and cunning.

[i]Wizards[/i] start out with a knowledge of magic, a selection of magical items, and a particular affinity for dweomercraft. Although seemingly weak and easy to overcome at first sight, an experienced Wizard is a deadly foe.
You may also choose the race of your character (within limits; most roles have restrictions on which races are eligible for them):

[i]Dwarves[/i] are smaller than humans or elves, but are stocky and solid individuals. Dwarves' most notable trait is their great expertise in mining and metalwork. Dwarvish armor is said to be second in quality not even to the mithril armor of the Elves.
[i]Elves[/i] are agile, quick, and perceptive; very little of what goes on will escape an Elf. The quality of Elven craftsmanship often gives them an advantage in arms and armor.

[i]Gnomes[/i] are smaller than but generally similar to dwarves. Gnomes are known to be expert miners, and it is known that a secret underground mine complex built by this race exists within the Mazes of Menace, filled with both riches and danger.

[i]Humans[/i] are by far the most common race of the surface world, and are thus the norm to which other races are often compared. Although they have no special abilities, they can succeed in any role.

[i]Orcs[/i] are a cruel and barbaric race that hate every living thing (including other orcs). Above all others, Orcs hate Elves with a passion unequalled, and will go out of their way to kill one at any opportunity. The armor and weapons fashioned by the Orcs are typically of inferior quality.

chapters.title: What do all those things on the screen mean?
paragraphs: On the screen is kept a map of where you have been and what you have seen on the current dungeon level; as you explore more of the level, it appears on the screen in front of you.

When NetHack's ancestor [i]rogue[/i] first appeared, its screen orientation was almost unique among computer fantasy games. Since then, screen orientation has become the norm rather than the exception; NetHack continues this fine tradition. Unlike text adventure games that accept commands in pseudo-English sentences and explain the results in words, NetHack commands are all one or two keystrokes and the results are displayed graphically on the screen. A minimum screen size of 24 lines by 80 columns is recommended; if the screen is larger, only a 21x80 section will be used for the map.
NetHack can even be played by blind players, with the assistance of Braille readers or speech synthesisers. Instructions for configuring NetHack for the blind are included later in this document.
NetHack generates a new dungeon every time you play it; even the authors still find it an entertaining and exciting game despite having won several times.

NetHack offers a variety of display options. The options available to you will vary from port to port, depending on the capabilities of your hardware and software, and whether various compile-time options were enabled when your executable was created. The three possible display options are: a monochrome character interface, a color character interface, and a graphical interface using small pictures called tiles. The two character interfaces allow fonts with other characters to be substituted, but the default assignments use standard ASCII characters to represent everything. There is no difference between the various display options with respect to game play. Because we cannot reproduce the tiles or colors in the Guidebook, and because it is common to all ports, we will use the default ASCII characters from the monochrome character display when referring to things you might see on the screen during your game.

In order to understand what is going on in NetHack, first you must understand what NetHack is doing with the screen. The NetHack screen replaces the “You see ...” descriptions of text adventure games. Figure 1 is a sample of what a NetHack screen might look like. The way the screen looks for you depends on your platform.

chapters.title: The status lines (bottom)
paragraphs: The bottom two (or three) lines of the screen contain several cryptic pieces of information describing your current status. Figure 1 shows the traditional two-line status area below the map. Figure 2 shows just the status area, when the [i]statuslines:3[/i] option has been set (not all interfaces support this option). If any status line becomes wider than the screen, you might not see all of it due to truncation. When the numbers grow bigger and multiple [i]conditions[/i] are present, the two-line format will run out of room on the second line, but [i]statuslines:2[/i] is the default because a basic 24-line terminal isn't tall enough for the third line.
Here are explanations of what the various status items mean:
[b]Title[/b] — Your character's name and professional ranking (based on role and [i]experience level[/i], see below).

[b]Strength[/b] — A measure of your character's strength; one of your six basic attributes. A human character's attributes can range from 3 to 18 inclusive; non-humans may exceed these limits (occasionally you may get super-strengths of the form 18/xx, and magic can also cause attributes to exceed the normal limits). The higher your strength, the stronger you are. Strength affects how successfully you perform physical tasks, how much damage you do in combat, and how much loot you can carry.
[b]Dexterity[/b] — Dexterity affects your chances to hit in combat, to avoid traps, and do other tasks requiring agility or manipulation of objects.

[b]Constitution[/b] — Constitution affects your ability to recover from injuries and other strains on your stamina. When strength is low or modest, constitution also affects how much you can carry. With sufficiently high strength, the contribution to carrying capacity from your constitution no longer matters.
[b]Intelligence[/b] — Intelligence affects your ability to cast spells and read spellbooks.
[b]Wisdom[/b] — Wisdom comes from your practical experience (especially when dealing with magic). It affects your magical energy.
[b]Charisma[/b] — Charisma affects how certain creatures react toward you. In particular, it can affect the prices shopkeepers offer you.

[b]Alignment[/b] — [b]Lawful[/b], [b]Neutral[/b], or [b]Chaotic[/b]. Often, Lawful is taken as good and Chaotic as evil, but legal and ethical do not always coincide. Your alignment influences how other monsters react toward you. Monsters of a like alignment are more likely to be non-aggressive, while those of an opposing alignment are more likely to be seriously offended at your presence.

[b]Dungeon Level[/b] — How deep you are in the dungeon. You start at level one and the number increases as you go deeper into the dungeon. Some levels are special, and are identified by a name and not a number. The Amulet of Yendor is reputed to be somewhere beneath the twentieth level.
[b]Gold[/b] — The number of gold pieces you are openly carrying. Gold which you have concealed in containers is not counted.

[b]Hit Points[/b] — Your current and maximum hit points. Hit points indicate how much damage you can take before you die. The more you get hit in a fight, the lower they get. You can regain hit points by resting, or by using certain magical items or spells. The number in parentheses is the maximum number your hit points can reach.
[b]Power[/b] — Spell points. This tells you how much mystic energy ([i]mana[/i]) you have available for spell casting. Again, resting will regenerate the amount available.

[b]Armor Class[/b] — A measure of how effectively your armor stops blows from unfriendly creatures. The lower this number is, the more effective the armor; it is quite possible to have negative armor class. See the [i]Armor[/i] subsection of [i]Objects[/i] for more information.

[b]Experience[/b] — Your current experience level. If the [i]showexp[/i] option is set, it will be followed by a slash and experience points. As you adventure, you gain experience points. At certain experience point totals, you gain an experience level. The more experienced you are, the better you fight and withstand magical attacks. (By the time your level reaches double digits, the usefulness of showing the points with it has dropped significantly. You can use the ‘[code]O[/code]’ command to turn [i]showexp[/i] off to avoid using up the limited status line space.)
[b]Time[/b] — The number of turns elapsed so far, displayed if you have the [i]time[/i] option set.
[b]Status[/b] — Hunger: your current hunger status. Values are [b]Satiated[/b], [b]Not Hungry[/b] (or [b]Normal[/b]), [b]Hungry[/b], [b]Weak[/b], and [b]Fainting[/b]. Not shown when [b]Normal[/b].

Encumbrance: an indication of how what you are carrying affects your ability to move. Values are [b]Unencumbered[/b], [b]Burdened[/b], [b]Stressed[/b], [b]Strained[/b], [b]Overtaxed[/b], and [b]Overloaded[/b]. Not shown when [b]Unencumbered[/b].

Fatal conditions: [b]Stone[/b] (aka [b]Petrifying[/b], turning to stone), [b]Slime[/b] (turning into green slime), [b]Strngl[/b] (being strangled), [b]FoodPois[/b] (suffering from acute food poisoning), [b]TermIll[/b] (suffering from a terminal illness).
Non-fatal conditions: [b]Blind[/b] (can't see), [b]Deaf[/b] (can't hear), [b]Stun[/b] (stunned), [b]Conf[/b] (confused), [b]Hallu[/b] (hallucinating).
Movement modifiers: [b]Lev[/b] (levitating), [b]Fly[/b] (flying), [b]Ride[/b] (riding).
Other conditions and modifiers exist, but there isn't enough room to display them with the other status fields.

The [code]#attributes[/code] command (default key [code]^X[/code]) will show all current status information in unabbreviated format. It also shows other information which might be included on the status lines if those had more room.

chapters.title: The message line (top)
paragraphs: The top line of the screen is reserved for messages that describe things that are impossible to represent visually. If you see a “[b]--More--[/b]” on the top line, this means that NetHack has another message to display on the screen, but it wants to make certain that you've read the one that is there first. To read the next message, just press the space bar.
To change how and what messages are shown on the message line, see “Configuring Message Types” and the [i]verbose[/i] option.

chapters.title: The map (rest of the screen)
paragraphs: The rest of the screen is the map of the level as you have explored it so far. Each symbol on the screen represents something. You can set various graphics options to change some of the symbols the game uses; otherwise, the game will use default symbols. Here is a list of what the default symbols mean:
[b][code]\-[/code][/b] — The horizontal or corner walls of a room, or an open east/west door.
[b][code]|[/code][/b] — The vertical walls of a room, or an open north/south door, or a grave.
[b][code].[/code][/b] — The floor of a room, or ice, or a doorless doorway, or the span of an open drawbridge.
[b][code]#[/code][/b] — A corridor, or iron bars, or a tree, or the portcullis of a closed drawbridge.
Note: engravings in corridors also appear as [code]#[/code] but are shown in a different color from normal corridor locations.
[b][code]>[/code][/b] — Stairs down: a way to the next level.
[b][code]<[/code][/b] — Stairs up: a way to the previous level.
[b][code]+[/code][/b] — A closed door, or a spellbook containing a spell you may be able to learn.
[b][code]@[/code][/b] — Your character or a human or an elf.
[b][code]$[/code][/b] — A pile of gold.
[b][code]^[/code][/b] — A trap (once you have detected it).
[b][code])[/code][/b] — A weapon.
[b][code][lb][/code][/b] — A suit or piece of armor.
[b][code]%[/code][/b] — Something edible (not necessarily healthy).
[b][code]?[/code][/b] — A scroll.
[b][code]/[/code][/b] — A wand.
[b][code]=[/code][/b] — A ring.
[b][code]![/code][/b] — A potion.
[b][code]([/code][/b] — A useful item (pick-axe, key, lamp...).
[b][code]"[/code][/b] — An amulet or a spider web.
[b][code]*[/code][/b] — A gem or rock (possibly valuable, possibly worthless).
[b][code]`[/code][/b] — A boulder or statue or an engraving on the floor of a room.
Note: statues are displayed as if they were the monsters they depict so won't appear as a [i]grave accent[/i] (aka [i]back-tick[/i]).
[b][code]0[/code][/b] — An iron ball.
[b][code]_[/code][/b] — An altar, or an iron chain.
[b][code]{[/code][/b] — A fountain or a sink.
[b][code]}[/code][/b] — A pool of water or moat or a wall of water or a pool of lava or a wall of lava.
[b][code]\\[/code][/b] — An opulent throne.
[b][code]a[/code]-[code]z[/code] [i]and[/i][/b] —
[b][code]A[/code]-[code]H[/code][code]J[/code]-[code]Z[/code] [i]and[/i][/b] —

[b][code]@&':;[/code][/b] — Letters and certain other symbols represent the various inhabitants of the Mazes of Menace. Watch out, they can be nasty and vicious. Sometimes, however, they can be helpful.

[b][code]I[/code][/b] — Rather than a specific type of monster, this marks the last known location of an invisible or otherwise unseen monster. Note that the monster could have moved. The ‘s’, ‘F’, and ‘m’ commands may be useful here.

[b][code]1[/code]-[code]5[/code][/b] — The digits 1 through 5 may be displayed, marking unseen monsters sensed via the [i]Warning[/i] attribute. Less dangerous monsters are indicated by lower values, more dangerous by higher values.
You need not memorize all these symbols; you can ask the game what any symbol represents with the ‘/’ command (see the next section for more info).

chapters.title: Commands
paragraphs: Commands can be initiated by typing one or two characters to which the command is bound to, or typing the command name in the extended commands entry. Some commands, like “search”, do not require that any more information be collected by NetHack. Other commands might require additional information, for example a direction, or an object to be used. For those commands that require additional information, NetHack will present you with either a menu of choices or with a command line prompt requesting information. Which you are presented with will depend chiefly on how you have set the [i]menustyle[/i] option.

For example, a common question, in the form “What do you want to use? [lb]a-zA-Z ?*]”, asks you to choose an object you are carrying. Here, “a-zA-Z” are the inventory letters of your possible choices. Typing ‘?’ gives you an inventory list of these items, so you can see what each letter refers to. In this example, there is also a ‘*’ indicating that you may choose an object not on the list, if you wanted to use something unexpected. Typing a ‘*’ lists your entire inventory, so you can see the inventory letters of every object you're carrying. Finally, if you change your mind and decide you don't want to do this command after all, you can press the ESC key to abort the command.

You can put a number before some commands to repeat them that many times; for example, “10s” will search ten times. If you have the [i]number_pad[/i] option set, you must type ‘n’ to prefix a count, so the example above would be typed “n10s” instead. Commands for which counts make no sense ignore them. In addition, movement commands can be prefixed for greater control (see below). To cancel a count or a prefix, press the ESC key.

The list of commands is rather long, but it can be read at any time during the game through the ‘?’ command, which accesses a menu of helpful texts. Here are the default key bindings for your reference:
[b]?[/b] — Help menu: display one of several help texts available.

[b]/[/b] — The “whatis” command, to tell what a symbol represents. You may choose to specify a location or type a symbol (or even a whole word) to explain. Specifying a location is done by moving the cursor to a particular spot on the map and then pressing one of ‘.’, ‘,’, ‘;’, or ‘:’. ‘.’ will explain the symbol at the chosen location, conditionally check for “More info?” depending upon whether the [i]help[/i] option is on, and then you will be asked to pick another location; ‘,’ will explain the symbol but skip any additional information, then let you pick another location; ‘;’ will skip additional info and also not bother asking you to choose another location to examine; ‘:’ will show additional info, if any, without asking for confirmation. When picking a location, pressing the ESC key will terminate this command, or pressing ‘?’ will give a brief reminder about how it works.

If the [i]autodescribe[/i] option is on, a short description of what you see at each location is shown as you move the cursor. Typing ‘#’ while picking a location will toggle that option on or off. The [i]whatis_coord[/i] option controls whether the short description includes map coordinates.
Specifying a name rather than a location always gives any additional information available about that name.

You may also request a description of nearby monsters, all monsters currently displayed, nearby objects, or all objects. The [i]whatis_coord[/i] option controls which format of map coordinate is included with their descriptions.
[b]&[/b] — Tell what a command does.
[b]<[/b] — Go up to the previous level (if you are on a staircase or ladder).
[b]>[/b] — Go down to the next level (if you are on a staircase or ladder).

[b][lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Go one step in the direction indicated (see Figure 3). If you sense or remember a monster there, you will fight the monster instead. Only these one-step movement commands cause you to fight monsters; the others (below) are “safe.” [code][/code]

Figure 3
[b][lb]YUHJKLBN][/b] — Go in that direction until you hit a wall or run into something.
[b]m[lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Prefix: move without picking up objects or fighting (even if you remember a monster there).

A few non-movement commands use the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix to request operating via menu (to temporarily override the [i]menustyle[/i][code]:traditional[/code] option). Primarily useful for ‘[code],[/code]’ (pickup) when there is only one class of objects present (where there won't be any “what kinds of objects?” prompt, so no opportunity to answer ‘m’ at that prompt).

The prefix will make “#travel” command show a menu of interesting targets in sight. It can also be used with the ‘[code]\[/code]’ (known, show a list of all discovered objects) and the ‘[code]`[/code]’ (knownclass, show a list of discovered objects in a particular class) commands to offer a menu of several sorting alternatives (which sets a new value for the [i]sortdiscoveries[/i] option); also for “#vanquished” and “#genocided” commands to offer a sorting menu.

A few other commands (eat food, offer sacrifice, apply tinning-kit, drink/quaff, dip, tip container) use the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix to skip checking for applicable objects on the floor and go straight to checking inventory, or (for “#loot” to remove a saddle), skip containers and go straight to adjacent monsters.
In debug mode (aka “wizard mode”), the ‘m’ prefix may also be used with the “#teleport” and “#wizlevelport” commands.
[b]F[lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Prefix: fight a monster (even if you only guess one is there).
[b]g[lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Prefix: move until something interesting is found.
[b]G[lb]yuhjklbn] or <Control>+[lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Prefix: similar to ‘g’, but forking of corridors is not considered interesting.

Note: <Control>+<key> means holding the <Control> or <Ctrl> key down like <Shift> while typing and releasing <key>, then releasing <Control>. ^<key> is used as shorthand elsewhere in the Guidebook to mean the same thing. Control characters are case-insensitive so ^x and ^X are the same.

[b]M[lb]yuhjklbn][/b] — Old versions supported ‘[code]M[/code]’ as a movement prefix which combined the effect of ‘[code]m[/code]’ with [code]<Control>[/code]+<direction>. That is no longer supported as a prefix but similar effect can be achieved by using ‘[code]m[/code]’ and [code]G[/code]<direction> in combination. [code]m[/code] can also be used in combination with [code]g[/code]<direction>, [code]<Control>[/code]+<direction>, or [code]<Shift>[/code]+<direction>.
[b]_[/b] — Travel to a map location via a shortest-path algorithm.

The shortest path is computed over map locations the hero knows about (e.g. seen or previously traversed). If there is no known path, a guess is made instead. Stops on most of the same conditions as the ‘[code]G[/code]’ prefix, but without picking up objects, so implicitly forces the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix. For ports with mouse support, the command is also invoked when a mouse-click takes place on a location other than the current position.
[b].[/b] — Wait or rest, do nothing for one turn. Precede with the ‘m’ prefix to wait for a turn even next to a hostile monster, if [i]safe_wait[/i] is on.
[b]a[/b] — Apply (use) a tool (pick-axe, key, lamp...).
If used on a wand, that wand will be broken, releasing its magic in the process. Confirmation is required.
[b]A[/b] — Remove one or more worn items, such as armor.
Use ‘T’ (take off) to take off only one piece of armor or ‘R’ (remove) to take off only one accessory.
[b]^A[/b] — Repeat the previous command.
[b]c[/b] — Close a door.
[b]C[/b] — Call (name) a monster, an individual object, or a type of object.
Same as extended command “#name”.
[b]^C[/b] — Panic button. Quit the game.
[b]d[/b] — Drop something.
For example “d7a” means drop seven items of object [i]a[/i].
[b]D[/b] — Drop several things.
In answer to the question
“What kinds of things do you want to drop? [lb]!%= BUCXPaium]”
you should type zero or more object symbols possibly followed by ‘a’ and/or ‘i’ and/or ‘u’ and/or ‘m’. In addition, one or more of the blessed/uncursed/cursed groups may be typed.
[indent][b]DB[/b] — drop all objects known to be blessed.[/indent]
[indent][b]DU[/b] — drop all objects known to be uncursed.[/indent]
[indent][b]DC[/b] — drop all objects known to be cursed.[/indent]
[indent][b]DX[/b] — drop all objects of unknown B/U/C status.[/indent]
[indent][b]DP[/b] — drop objects picked up last.[/indent]
[indent][b]Da[/b] — drop all objects, without asking for confirmation.[/indent]
[indent][b]Di[/b] — examine your inventory before dropping anything.[/indent]
[indent][b]Du[/b] — drop only unpaid objects (when in a shop).[/indent]
[indent][b]Dm[/b] — use a menu to pick which object(s) to drop.[/indent]
[indent][b]D%u[/b] — drop only unpaid food.[/indent]

The last example shows a combination. There are four categories of object filtering: class (‘!’ for potions, ‘?’ for scrolls, and so on), shop status (‘u’ for unpaid, in other words, owned by the shop), bless/curse state (‘B’, ‘U’, ‘C’, and ‘X’ as shown above), and novelty (‘P’, recently picked up items; controlled by picking up or dropping things rather than by any time factor).

If you specify more than one value in a category (such as “!?” for potions and scrolls or “BU” for blessed and uncursed), an inventory object will meet the criteria if it matches any of the specified values (so “!?” means ‘!’ or ‘?’). If you specify more than one category, an inventory object must meet each of the category criteria (so “%u” means class ‘%’ and unpaid ‘u’). Lastly, you may specify multiple values within multiple categories: “!?BU” will select all potions and scrolls which are known to be blessed or uncursed. (In versions prior to 3.6, filter combinations behaved differently.)
[b]^D[/b] — Kick something (usually a door).
[b]e[/b] — Eat food.

Normally checks for edible item(s) on the floor, then if none are found or none are chosen, checks for edible item(s) in inventory. Precede ‘e’ with the ‘m’ prefix to bypass attempting to eat anything off the floor.

If you attempt to eat while already satiated, you might choke to death. If you risk it, you will be asked whether to “continue eating?” [i]if you survive the first bite[/i]. You can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:eating[/i] option to require a response of [code]yes[/code] instead of just [code]y[/code].
[b]E[/b] — Engrave a message on the floor.
[code]E- - write in the dust with your fingers.[/code]
Engraving the word “Elbereth” will cause most monsters to not attack you hand-to-hand (but if you attack, you will rub it out); this is often useful to give yourself a breather.

[b]f[/b] — Fire (shoot or throw) one of the objects placed in your quiver (or quiver sack, or that you have at the ready). You may select ammunition with a previous ‘Q’ command, or let the computer pick something appropriate if [i]autoquiver[/i] is true. If your wielded weapon has the throw-and-return property, your quiver is empty, and [i]autoquiver[/i] is false, you will throw that wielded weapon instead of filling the quiver. This will also automatically use a polearm if wielded. If [i]fireassist[/i] is true, firing will automatically try to wield a launcher (for example, a bow or a sling) matching the ammo in the quiver; this might take multiple turns, and get interrupted by a monster. Remember to swap back to your main melee weapon afterwards.
See also ‘t’ (throw) for more general throwing and shooting.
[b]i[/b] — List your inventory (everything you're carrying).
[b]I[/b] — List selected parts of your inventory, usually be specifying the character for a particular set of objects, like ‘[lb]’ for armor or ‘!’ for potions.
[indent][b]I*[/b] — list all gems in inventory;[/indent]
[indent][b]Iu[/b] — list all unpaid items;[/indent]
[indent][b]Ix[/b] — list all used up items that are on your shopping bill;[/indent]
[indent][b]IB[/b] — list all items known to be blessed;[/indent]
[indent][b]IU[/b] — list all items known to be uncursed;[/indent]
[indent][b]IC[/b] — list all items known to be cursed;[/indent]
[indent][b]IX[/b] — list all items whose bless/curse status is unknown;[/indent]
[indent][b]IP[/b] — list items picked up last;[/indent]
[indent][b]I$[/b] — count your money.[/indent]
[b]o[/b] — Open a door.
[b]O[/b] — Set options.

A menu showing the current option values will be displayed. You can change most values simply by selecting the menu entry for the given option (ie, by typing its letter or clicking upon it, depending on your user interface). For the non-boolean choices, a further menu or prompt will appear once you've closed this menu. The available options are listed later in this Guidebook. Options are usually set before the game rather than with the ‘O’ command; see the section on options below. Precede ‘O’ with the ‘m’ prefix to show advanced options.
[b]^O[/b] — Show overview.
Shortcut for “#overview”: list interesting dungeon levels visited.
(Prior to 3.6.0, ‘^O’ was a debug mode command which listed the placement of all special levels. Use “#wizwhere” to run that command.)
[b]p[/b] — Pay your shopping bill.
[b]P[/b] — Put on an accessory (ring, amulet, or blindfold).

This command may also be used to wear armor. The prompt for which inventory item to use will only list accessories, but choosing an unlisted item of armor will attempt to wear it. (See the ‘W’ command below. It lists armor as the inventory choices but will accept an accessory and attempt to put that on.)
[b]^P[/b] — Repeat previous message.
Subsequent ‘^P’s repeat earlier messages. For some interfaces, the behavior can be varied via the [i]msg_window[/i] option.
[b]q[/b] — Quaff (drink) something (potion, water, etc).

When there is a fountain or sink present, it asks whether to drink from that. If that is declined, then it offers a chance to choose a potion from inventory. Precede ‘q’ with the ‘m’ prefix to skip asking about drinking from a fountain or sink.
[b]Q[/b] — Select an object for your quiver, quiver sack, or just generally at the ready (only one of these is available at a time). You can then throw this (or one of these) using the ‘f’ command.
[b]r[/b] — Read a scroll or spellbook.
[b]R[/b] — Remove a worn accessory (ring, amulet, or blindfold).

If you're wearing more than one, you'll be prompted for which one to remove. When you're only wearing one, then by default it will be removed without asking, but you can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:Remove[/i] option to require a prompt.

This command may also be used to take off armor. The prompt for which inventory item to remove only lists worn accessories, but an item of worn armor can be chosen. (See the ‘T’ command below. It lists armor as the inventory choices but will accept an accessory and attempt to remove it.)
[b]^R[/b] — Redraw the screen.

[b]s[/b] — Search for secret doors and traps around you. It usually takes several tries to find something. Precede with the ‘m’ prefix to search for a turn even next to a hostile monster, if [i]safe_wait[/i] is on.
Can also be used to figure out whether there is still a monster at an adjacent “remembered, unseen monster” marker.
[b]S[/b] — Save the game (which suspends play and exits the program). The saved game will be restored automatically the next time you play using the same character name.

In normal play, once a saved game is restored the file used to hold the saved data is deleted. In explore mode, once restoration is accomplished you are asked whether to keep or delete the file. Keeping the file makes it feasible to play for a while then quit without saving and later restore again.
There is no “save current game state and keep playing” command, not even in explore mode where saved game files can be kept and re-used.
[b]t[/b] — Throw an object or shoot a projectile.

There's no separate “shoot” command. If you throw an arrow while wielding a bow, you are shooting that arrow and any weapon skill bonus or penalty for bow applies. If you throw an arrow while not wielding a bow, you are throwing it by hand and it will generally be less effective than when shot.
See also ‘f’ (fire) for throwing or shooting an item pre-selected via the ‘Q’ (quiver) command, with some extra assistance.
[b]T[/b] — Take off armor.

If you're wearing more than one piece, you'll be prompted for which one to take off. (Note that this treats a cloak covering a suit and/or a shirt, or a suit covering a shirt, as if the underlying items weren't there.) When you're only wearing one, then by default it will be taken off without asking, but you can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:Remove[/i] option to require a prompt.

This command may also be used to remove accessories. The prompt for which inventory item to take off only lists worn armor, but a worn accessory can be chosen. (See the ‘R’ command above. It lists accessories as the inventory choices but will accept an item of armor and attempt to take it off.)
[b]^T[/b] — Teleport, if you have the ability.
[b]v[/b] — Display a list of significant events in the current game, also shown by [code]#chronicle[/code].
‘[code]v[/code]’ used to display the game's version number. Use ‘[code]V[/code]’ for that now.
[b]V[/b] — Display version number.
‘[code]V[/code]’ used to display a summary of the game's history. Still available via [code]#history[/code].
[b]w[/b] — Wield weapon.
[code]w- - wield nothing, use your bare (or gloved) hands.[/code]
Some characters can wield two weapons at once; use the ‘X’ command (or the “#twoweapon” extended command) to do so.
[b]W[/b] — Wear armor.

This command may also be used to put on an accessory (ring, amulet, or blindfold). The prompt for which inventory item to use will only list armor, but choosing an unlisted accessory will attempt to put it on. (See the ‘P’ command above. It lists accessories as the inventory choices but will accept an item of armor and attempt to wear it.)
[b]x[/b] — Exchange your wielded weapon with the item in your alternate weapon slot.
The latter is used as your secondary weapon when engaging in two-weapon combat. Note that if one of these slots is empty, the exchange still takes place.
[b]X[/b] — Toggle two-weapon combat, if your character can do it. Also available via the “#twoweapon” extended command.
(In versions prior to 3.6 this keystroke ran the command to switch from normal play to “explore mode”, also known as “discovery mode”, which has now been moved to “#exploremode” and M-X.)
[b]^X[/b] — Display basic information about your character.

Displays name, role, race, gender (unless role name makes that redundant, such as [i]Caveman[/i] or [i]Priestess[/i]), and alignment, along with your patron deity and his or her opposition. It also shows most of the various items of information from the status line(s) in a less terse form, including several additional things which don't appear in the normal status display due to space considerations.
In normal play, that's all that ‘^X’ displays. In explore mode, the role and status feedback is augmented by the information provided by [i]enlightenment[/i] magic.
[b]z[/b] — Zap a wand.
[code]z. - to aim at yourself, use ‘.’ for the direction.[/code]
[b]Z[/b] — Zap (cast) a spell.
[code]Z. - to cast at yourself, use ‘.’ for the direction.[/code]
[b]^Z[/b] — Suspend the game UNIX versions with job control only). See “#suspend” below for more details.
[b]:[/b] — Look at what is here.
[b];[/b] — Show what type of thing a visible symbol corresponds to.
[b],[/b] — Pick up some things from the floor beneath you.
May be preceded by ‘m’ to force a selection menu.
[b]@[/b] — Toggle the [i]autopickup[/i] option on and off.
[b]^[/b] — Ask for the type of an adjacent trap you found earlier.
[b])[/b] — Tell what weapon you are wielding.
[b][lb][/b] — Tell what armor you are wearing.
[b]=[/b] — Tell what rings you are wearing.
[b]"[/b] — Tell what amulet you are wearing.
[b]([/b] — Tell what tools you are using.
[b]*[/b] — Tell what equipment you are using.
Combines the preceding five type-specific commands into one.
[b]$[/b] — Report the gold you're carrying, possibly shop credit and/or debt too.
[b]+[/b] — List the spells you know.

Using this command, you can also rearrange the order in which your spells are listed, either by sorting the entire list or by picking one spell from the menu then picking another to swap places with it. Swapping pairs of spells changes their casting letters, so the change lasts after the current ‘+’ command finishes. Sorting the whole list is temporary. To make the most recent sort order persist beyond the current ‘+’ command, choose the sort option again and then pick “reassign casting letters”. (Any spells learned after that will be added to the end of the list rather than be inserted into the sorted ordering.)
[b]\\[/b] — Show what types of objects have been discovered.
May be preceded by ‘[code]m[/code]’ to select preferred display order.
[b]`[/b] — Show discovered types for one class of objects.
May be preceded by ‘[code]m[/code]’ to select preferred display order.
[b]|[/b] — If persistent inventory display is supported and enabled (with the [i]perm_invent[/i] option), interact with it instead of with the map.

Allows scrolling with the menu_first_page, menu_previous_page, menu_next_page, and menu_last_page keys (‘[code]^[/code]’, ‘[code]<[/code]’, ‘[code]>[/code]’, ‘[code]|[/code]’ by default). Some interfaces also support menu_shift_left and menu_shift_right keys (‘[code]{[/code]’ and ‘[code]}[/code]’ by default). Use the [i]Return[/i] (aka [i]Enter[/i]) or [i]Escape[/i] key to resume play.
[b]![/b] — Escape to a shell. See “#shell” below for more details.
[b]Del[/b] — Show map without obstructions. You can view the explored portion of the current level's map without monsters; without monsters and objects; or without monsters, objects, and traps.
The <del> key is also shown as <delete> on some keyboards or <rubout> on others. It is sometimes displayed as ^? even though that is not an actual control character.
Many terminals have an option to swap the <delete> and <backspace> keys, so typing the <del> key might not execute this command. If that happens, you can use the extended command “#terrain” instead.
[b]#[/b] — Perform an extended command.

As you can see, the authors of NetHack used up all the letters, so this is a way to introduce the less frequently used commands. What extended commands are available depends on what features the game was compiled with.
[b]#adjust[/b] — Adjust inventory letters (most useful when the [i]fixinv[/i] option is “on”). Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-a’.

This command allows you to move an item from one particular inventory slot to another so that it has a letter which is more meaningful for you or that it will appear in a particular location when inventory listings are displayed. You can move to a currently empty slot, or if the destination is occupied—and won't merge—the item there will swap slots with the one being moved. “#adjust” can also be used to split a stack of objects; when choosing the item to adjust, enter a count prior to its letter.

Adjusting without a count used to collect all compatible stacks when moving to the destination. That behavior has been changed; to gather compatible stacks, “#adjust” a stack into its own inventory slot. If it has a name assigned, other stacks with the same name or with no name will merge provided that all their other attributes match. If it does not have a name, only other stacks with no name are eligible. In either case, otherwise compatible stacks with a different name will not be merged. This contrasts with using “#adjust” to move from one slot to a different slot. In that situation, moving (no count given) a compatible stack will merge if either stack has a name when the other doesn't and give that name to the result, while splitting (count given) will ignore the source stack's name when deciding whether to merge with the destination stack.

[b]#annotate[/b] — Allows you to specify one line of text to associate with the current dungeon level. All levels with annotations are displayed by the “#overview” command. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-A’, and also ‘^N’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
Preceding #annotate with the ‘m’ prefix is the same as #overview with the prefix.
[b]#apply[/b] — Apply (use) a tool such as a pick-axe, a key, or a lamp. Default key is ‘a’.
If the tool used acts on items on the floor, using the ‘m’ prefix skips those items.
If used on a wand, that wand will be broken, releasing its magic in the process. Confirmation is required.
[b]#attributes[/b] — Show your attributes. Default key is ‘^X’.
[b]#autopickup[/b] — Toggle the [i]autopickup[/i] option on/off. Default key is ‘@’.

[b]#bugreport[/b] — Bring up a browser window to submit a report to the NetHack Development Team. Can be disabled at the time the program is built; when enabled, CRASHREPORTURL must be set in the system configuration file.
[b]#call[/b] — Call (name) a monster, or an object in inventory, on the floor, or in the discoveries list, or add an annotation for the current level (same as “#annotate”). Default key is ‘C’.
[b]#cast[/b] — Cast a spell. Default key is ‘Z’.
[b]#chat[/b] — Talk to someone. Default key is ‘M-c’.
[b]#chronicle[/b] — Show a list of important game events. Default key is ‘v’.
[b]#close[/b] — Close a door. Default key is ‘c’.
[b]#conduct[/b] — List voluntary challenges you have maintained. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-C’.
See the section below entitled “Conduct” for details.
[b]#debugfuzzer[/b] — Start the fuzz tester. Debug mode only.
[b]#dip[/b] — Dip an object into something. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-d’.
The ‘m’ prefix skips dipping into a fountain or pool if there is one at your location.
[b]#down[/b] — Go down a staircase. Default key is ‘>’.
[b]#drop[/b] — Drop an item. Default key is ‘d’.
[b]#droptype[/b] — Drop specific item types. Default key is ‘D’.
[b]#eat[/b] — Eat something. Default key is ‘e’. The ‘m’ prefix skips eating items on the floor.
[b]#engrave[/b] — Engrave writing on the floor. Default key is ‘E’.
[b]#enhance[/b] — Advance or check weapon and spell skills. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-e’.
[b]#exploremode[/b] — Switch from normal play to non-scoring explore mode. Default key is ‘M-X’.

Requires confirmation; default response is [code]n[/code] (no). To really switch to explore mode, respond with [code]y[/code]. You can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:quit[/i] option to require a response of [code]yes[/code] instead.
[b]#fight[/b] — Prefix key to force fight a direction, even if you see nothing to fight there. Default key is ‘F’, or ‘-’ with [i]number_pad[/i]
[b]#fire[/b] — Fire ammunition from quiver, possibly autowielding a launcher, or hit with a wielded polearm. Default key is ‘f’.
[b]#force[/b] — Force a lock. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-f’.
[b]#genocided[/b] — List any monster types which have been genocided. In explore mode and debug mode it also shows types which have become extinct.
The display order is the same as is used by #vanquished. The ‘m’ prefix brings up a menu of available sorting orders, and doing that for either #genocided or #vanquished changes the order for both.

If the sorting order is “count high to low” or “count low to high” (which are applicable for #vanquished), that will be ignored for #genocided and alphabetical will be used instead. The menu omits those two choices when used for #genocide.
Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-g’.
[b]#glance[/b] — Show what type of thing a map symbol corresponds to. Default key is ‘;’.
[b]#help[/b] — Show the help menu. Default key is ‘?’, and also ‘h’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.

[b]#herecmdmenu[/b] — Show a menu of possible actions directed at your current location. The menu is limited to a subset of the likeliest actions, not an exhaustive set of all possibilities. Autocompletes.
If mouse support is enabled and the [i]herecmd_menu[/i] option is On, clicking on the hero (or steed when mounted) will execute this command.
[b]#history[/b] — Show a summary of the game's development.
[b]#inventory[/b] — Show your inventory. Default key is ‘i’.
[b]#inventtype[/b] — Inventory specific item types. Default key is ‘I’.
[b]#invoke[/b] — Invoke an object's special powers. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-i’.
[b]#jump[/b] — Jump to another location. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-j’, and also ‘j’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
[b]#kick[/b] — Kick something. Default key is ‘^D’, and ‘k’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
[b]#known[/b] — Show what object types have been discovered. Default key is ‘[code]\[/code]’.
The ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix allows assigning a new value to the [i]sortdiscoveries[/i] option to control the order in which the discoveries are displayed.
[b]#knownclass[/b] — Show discovered types for one class of objects. Default key is ‘[code]`[/code]’.
The ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix operates the same as for “#known”.
[b]#levelchange[/b] — Change your experience level. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#lightsources[/b] — Show mobile light sources. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#look[/b] — Look at what is here, under you. Default key is ‘:’.
[b]#lookaround[/b] — Describe what you can see, or remember, of your surroundings.

[b]#loot[/b] — Loot a box or bag on the floor beneath you, or the saddle from a steed standing next to you. Autocompletes. Precede with the ‘m’ prefix to skip containers at your location and go directly to removing a saddle. Default key is ‘M-l’, and also ‘l’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
[b]#monster[/b] — Use a monster's special ability (when polymorphed into monster form). Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-m’.
[b]#name[/b] — Name a monster, an individual object, or a type of object. Same as “#call”. Autocompletes. Default keys are ‘N’, ‘M-n’, and ‘M-N’.
[b]#offer[/b] — Offer a sacrifice to the gods. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-o’.
You'll need to find an altar to have any chance at success. Corpses of recently killed monsters are the fodder of choice.
The ‘m’ prefix skips offering any items which are on the altar.
[b]#open[/b] — Open a door. Default key is ‘o’.
[b]#options[/b] — Show and change option settings. Default key is ‘O’. Precede with the ‘m’ prefix to show advanced options.

[b]#optionsfull[/b] — Show advanced game option settings. No default key. Precede with the ‘m’ prefix to execute the simpler options command. (Mainly useful if you use [code]BINDING=O:optionsfull[/code] to switch ‘[code]O[/code]’ from simple options back to traditional advanced options.)

[b]#overview[/b] — Display information you've discovered about the dungeon. Any visited level with an annotation is included, and many things (altars, thrones, fountains, and so on; extra stairs leading to another dungeon branch) trigger an automatic annotation. If dungeon overview is chosen during end-of-game disclosure, every visited level will be included regardless of annotations.

Precede #overview with the ‘m’ prefix to display the dungeon overview as a menu where you can select any visited level to add or remove an annotation without needing to return to that level. This will also force all visited levels to be displayed rather than just the “interesting” subset.
Autocompletes. Default keys are ‘^O’, and ‘M-O’.
[b]#panic[/b] — Test the panic routine. Terminates the current game. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.

Asks for confirmation; default is [code]n[/code] (no); continue playing. To really panic, respond with [code]y[/code]. You can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:quit[/i] option to require a response of [code]yes[/code] instead.
[b]#pay[/b] — Pay your shopping bill. Default key is ‘p’.

[b]#perminv[/b] — If persistent inventory display is supported and enabled (with the [i]perm_invent[/i] option), interact with it instead of with the map. You'll be prompted for menu scrolling keystrokes such as ‘[code]>[/code]’ and ‘[code]<[/code]’. Press [code]Return[/code] or [code]Escape[/code] to resume normal play. Default key is ‘|’.
[b]#pickup[/b] — Pick up things at the current location. Default key is ‘,’. The ‘m’ prefix forces use of a menu.
[b]#polyself[/b] — Polymorph self. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#pray[/b] — Pray to the gods for help. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-p’.

Praying too soon after receiving prior help is a bad idea. (Hint: entering the dungeon alive is treated as having received help. You probably shouldn't start off a new game by praying right away.) Since using this command by accident can cause trouble, there is an option to make you confirm your intent before praying. It is enabled by default, and you can reset the [i]paranoid_confirmation[/i] option to disable it.
[b]#prevmsg[/b] — Show previously displayed game messages. Default key is ‘^P’.
[b]#puton[/b] — Put on an accessory (ring, amulet, etc). Default key is ‘P’.
[b]#quaff[/b] — Quaff (drink) something. Default key is ‘q’.
The ‘m’ prefix skips drinking from a fountain or sink if there is one at your location.
[b]#quit[/b] — Quit the program without saving your game. Autocompletes.

Since using this command by accident would throw away the current game, you are asked to confirm your intent before quitting. Default response is [code]n[/code] (no); continue playing. To really quit, respond with [code]y[/code]. You can set the [i]paranoid_confirmation:quit[/i] option to require a response of [code]yes[/code] instead.
[b]#quiver[/b] — Select ammunition for quiver. Default key is ‘Q’.
[b]#read[/b] — Read a scroll, a spellbook, or something else. Default key is ‘r’.
[b]#redraw[/b] — Redraw the screen. Default key is ‘^R’, and also ‘^L’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
[b]#remove[/b] — Remove an accessory (ring, amulet, etc). Default key is ‘R’.
[b]#repeat[/b] — Repeat the previous command. Default key is ‘^A’.
[b]#reqmenu[/b] — Prefix key to modify the behavior or request menu from some commands. Prevents autopickup when used with movement commands. Default key is ‘m’.
[b]#retravel[/b] — Travel to a previously selected travel destination. Default key is ‘C-_’. See also #travel.
[b]#ride[/b] — Ride (or stop riding) a saddled creature. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-R’.
[b]#rub[/b] — Rub a lamp or a stone. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-r’.
[b]#run[/b] — Prefix key to run towards a direction. Default key is ‘G’ when [i]number_pad[/i] is off, ‘5’ when [i]number_pad[/i] is set to 1 or 3, otherwise ‘M-5’ when it is set to 2 or 4.
[b]#rush[/b] — Prefix key to rush towards a direction. Default is ‘g’ when [i]number_pad[/i] is off, ‘M-5’ when [i]number_pad[/i] is set to 1 or 3, otherwise ‘5’ when it is set to 2 or 4.
[b]#save[/b] — Save the game and exit the program. Default key is ‘S’.
[b]#saveoptions[/b] — Save configuration options to the config file. This will overwrite the file, removing all comments, so if you have manually edited the config file, don't use this.
[b]#search[/b] — Search for traps and secret doors around you. Default key is ‘s’.
[b]#seeall[/b] — Show all equipment in use. Default key is ‘*’.
Will display in-use items in a menu even when there is only one.
[b]#seeamulet[/b] — Show the amulet currently worn. Default key is ‘"’.
Using the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix will force the display of a worn amulet in a menu rather than with just a message.
[b]#seearmor[/b] — Show the armor currently worn. Default key is ‘[lb]’.
Will display worn armor in a menu even when there is only thing worn.
[b]#seerings[/b] — Show the ring(s) currently worn. Default key is ‘=’.
Will display worn rings in a menu if there are two (or there is just one and is a meat ring rather than a “real” ring). Use the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix to force a menu for one ring.
[b]#seetools[/b] — Show the tools currently in use. Default key is ‘(’.

Will display the result in a message if there is one tool in use (worn blindfold or towel or lenses, lit lamp(s) and/or candle(s), leashes attached to pets). Will display a menu if there are more than one or if the command is preceded by the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix.
[b]#seeweapon[/b] — Show the weapon currently wielded. Default key is ‘)’.

If dual-wielding, a separate message about the secondary weapon will be given. Using the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix will force a menu and it will include primary weapon, alternate weapon even when not dual-wielding, and also whatever is currently assigned to the quiver slot.

[b]#shell[/b] — Do a shell escape, switching from NetHack to a subprocess. Can be disabled at the time the program is built. When enabled, access for specific users can be controlled by the system configuration file. Use the shell command ‘[code]exit[/code]’ to return to the game. Default key is ‘!’.

[b]#showgold[/b] — Report the gold in your inventory, including gold you know about in containers you're carrying. If you are inside a shop, report any credit or debt you have in that shop. Default key is ‘$’.
[b]#showspells[/b] — List and reorder known spells. Default key is ‘+’.

[b]#showtrap[/b] — Describe an adjacent trap, possibly covered by objects or a monster. To be eligible, the trap must already be discovered. (The “#terrain” command can display your map with all objects and monsters temporarily removed, making it possible to see all discovered traps.) Default key is ‘^’.
[b]#sit[/b] — Sit down. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-s’.
[b]#stats[/b] — Show memory usage statistics. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.

[b]#suspend[/b] — Suspend the game, switching from NetHack to the terminal it was started from without performing save-and-exit. Can be disabled at the time the program is built. When enabled, mainly useful for [i]tty[/i] and [i]curses[/i] interfaces on UNIX. Use the shell command ‘[code]fg[/code]’ to return to the game. Default key is ‘^Z’.
[b]#swap[/b] — Swap wielded and secondary weapons. Default key is ‘x’.
[b]#takeoff[/b] — Take off one piece of armor. Default key is ‘T’.
[b]#takeoffall[/b] — Remove all armor. Default key is ‘A’.
[b]#teleport[/b] — Teleport around the level. Default key is ‘^T’.

[b]#terrain[/b] — Show map without obstructions. In normal play you can view the explored portion of the current level's map without monsters; without monsters and objects; or without monsters, objects, and traps.
If there are visible clouds of gas in view, they are treated like traps when deciding whether to show them or the floor underneath them.
In explore mode, you can choose to view the full map rather than just its explored portion. In debug mode there are additional choices.
Autocompletes. Default key is ‘<del>’ or ‘<delete>’ (see [i]Del[/i] above).

[b]#therecmdmenu[/b] — Show a menu of possible actions directed at a location next to you. The menu is limited to a subset of the likeliest actions, not an exhaustive set of all possibilities. Autocompletes.
[b]#throw[/b] — Throw something. Default key is ‘t’.
[b]#timeout[/b] — Look at the timeout queue. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.

[b]#tip[/b] — Tip over a container (bag or box) to pour out its contents. When there are containers on the floor, the game will prompt to pick one of them or “tip something being carried”. If the latter is chosen, there will be another prompt for which item from inventory to tip.

The ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix makes the command skip containers on the floor and pick one from inventory, except for the special case of [i]menustyle[/i][code]:traditional[/code] with two or more containers present; that situation will start with the floor container menu.
Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-T’.
[b]#toggle[/b] — Toggle a boolean option on or off. Requires a parameter in parenthesis, the name of the option to toggle. The option must be settable in-game.
For example:

[code]BIND=':toggle(price_quotes)
BIND=@:toggle(autopickup)[/code]

[b]#travel[/b] — Travel to a specific location on the map. Default key is ‘_’. Using the “request menu” prefix shows a menu of interesting targets in sight without asking to move the cursor. When picking a target with cursor and the [i]autodescribe[/i] option is on, the top line will show “(no travel path)” if your character does not know of a path to that location. See also #retravel.
[b]#turn[/b] — Turn undead away. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-t’.
[b]#twoweapon[/b] — Toggle two-weapon combat on or off. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘X’, and also ‘M-2’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is off.
Note that you must use suitable weapons for this type of combat, or it will be automatically turned off.
[b]#untrap[/b] — Untrap something (trap, door, or chest). Default key is ‘M-u’, and ‘u’ if [i]number_pad[/i] is on.
In some circumstances it can also be used to rescue trapped monsters.
[b]#up[/b] — Go up a staircase. Default key is ‘<’.
[b]#vanquished[/b] — List vanquished monsters by type and count.

Note that the vanquished monsters list includes all monsters killed by traps and each other as well as by you, and omits any which got removed from the game without being killed (perhaps by genocide, or by a mollified shopkeeper dismissing summoned Kops) or were already corpses when placed on the map.

Using the “request menu” prefix prior to #vanquished brings up a menu of sorting orders available (provided that the vanquished monsters list contains at least two types of monsters). Whichever ordering is picked gets assigned to the [i]sortvanquished[/i] option so is remembered for subsequent #vanquished requests. The “#genocided” command shares this sorting order.
During end-of-game disclosure, when asked whether to show vanquished monsters answering ‘[code]a[/code]’ will let you choose from the sort menu.
Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-V’.
[b]#version[/b] — Print compile time options for this version of NetHack.

The second paragraph lists the user interface(s) that are included. If there are more than one, you can use the [i]windowtype[/i] option in your run-time configuration file to select the one you want.
Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-v’.
[b]#versionshort[/b] — Show the program's version number, plus the date and time that the running copy was built from sources (not the version's release date). Default key is ‘V’.
[b]#vision[/b] — Show vision array. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wait[/b] — Rest one move while doing nothing. Default key is ‘.’, and also ‘ ’ if [i]rest_on_space[/i] is on.
[b]#wear[/b] — Wear a piece of armor. Default key is ‘W’.
[b]#whatdoes[/b] — Tell what a key does. Default key is ‘&’.
[b]#whatis[/b] — Show what type of thing a symbol corresponds to. Default key is ‘/’.
[b]#wield[/b] — Wield a weapon. Default key is ‘w’.
[b]#wipe[/b] — Wipe off your face. Autocompletes. Default key is ‘M-w’.
[b]#wizborn[/b] — Show monster birth, death, genocide, and extinct statistics. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizbury[/b] — Bury objects under and around you. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizcast[/b] — Cast any spell. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizdetect[/b] — Reveal hidden things (secret doors or traps or unseen monsters) within a modest radius. No time elapses. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^E’.
[b]#wizgenesis[/b] — Create a monster. May be prefixed by a count to create more than one. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^G’.
[b]#wizidentify[/b] — Identify all items in inventory. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^I’.
[b]#wizintrinsic[/b] — Set one or more intrinsic attributes. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.

[b]#wizkill[/b] — Remove monsters from play by just pointing at them. By default the hero gets credit or blame for killing the targets. Precede this command with the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix to override that. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizlevelport[/b] — Teleport to another level. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^V’.
[b]#wizmap[/b] — Map the level. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^F’.
[b]#wizrumorcheck[/b] — Verify rumor boundaries by displaying first and last true rumors and first and last false rumors.
Also displays first, second, and last random engravings, epitaphs, and hallucinatory monsters.
Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizseenv[/b] — Show map locations' seen vectors. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizsmell[/b] — Smell monster. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizwhere[/b] — Show locations of special levels. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#wizwish[/b] — Wish for something. Autocompletes. Debug mode only. Default key is ‘^W’. Precede this command with the ‘[code]m[/code]’ prefix to show a wish history menu.
[b]#wmode[/b] — Show wall modes. Autocompletes. Debug mode only.
[b]#zap[/b] — Zap a wand. Default key is ‘z’.
[b]#?[/b] — Help menu: get the list of available extended commands.

If your keyboard has a meta key (which, when pressed in combination with another key, modifies it by setting the “meta” [lb]8th, or “high”] bit), you can invoke many extended commands by meta-ing the first letter of the command.

On [i]Windows[/i] and [i]MS-DOS[/i], the “Alt” key can be used in this fashion. On other systems, if typing “Alt” plus another key transmits a two character sequence consisting of an [b]Escape[/b] followed by the other key, you may set the [i]altmeta[/i] option to have NetHack combine them into meta+<key>. (This combining action only takes place when NetHack is expecting a command to execute, not when accepting input to name something or to make a wish.)

Unlike control characters, where ^x and ^X denote the same thing, meta characters are case-sensitive: M-x and M-X represent different things. Some commands which can be run via a meta character require that the letter be capitalized because the lower-case equivalent is used for another command, so the three key combination meta+Shift+<letter> is needed.
